findings.claim: Vary how the parts are combined, not the parts. Goals that recombine the same subproblems (modularly varying goals, MVG) evolved modular circuits and reused motifs. Goals with no shared structure produced non-modular networks that re-evolve from scratch at each switch.
findings.evidence: Kashtan & Alon 2005 (full text, https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0503610102). Switching (X XOR Y) AND (Z XOR W) <-> ... OR ... every E = 20 generations solved 50/50 runs in <10,000 generations (mean 1,400 +- 1,000). Under a fixed goal, 36/50 runs solved within 1e5 generations (successful runs took ~9,000). MVG circuits had Qm = 0.54 against ~0 for fixed-goal circuits. They re-adapted within ~5 generations of a switch (~3 for the neural networks), often by changing one threshold. Random varying goals gave nonmodular circuits that 'forget'. A modular circuit placed under a fixed goal with a slight size penalty lost its modularity within tens of generations.

findings.claim: Switching over time is what works. Scoring many goals at once (the multiobjective control) gave virtually no speedup. So the planned per-life task family (L1) is not MVG, and should not be expected to break plateaus by itself.
findings.evidence: Kashtan, Noor & Alon 2007 (opened at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1948871/). Quote: 'the multiobjective scenarios showed virtually no speedup, whereas the equivalent MVG scenario showed speedup'. MVG speedup was about 10x for NAND circuits, up to 1e3 for feed-forward logic and 700 +- 450 for the hardest neural-network goals. It scales as S ~ T_fixed^alpha with alpha 0.7-1.0, so the harder the goal, the larger the speedup. Random goals with new targets (RVGv) gave a smaller speedup; alternating with one constant random goal (RVGc) slowed evolution for all goals.

findings.claim: How often to switch, between generations: the period must be longer than the time to re-adapt to each goal and shorter than the time to solve a fixed goal. The useful window spans orders of magnitude. Switching too fast or too slow both give rigid structures, and MVG's modularity effect fades with slow switching.
findings.evidence: Kashtan 2007: 'the switching time of the goals should be larger than the minimal time it takes to rewire the networks to achieve each new goal and shorter than the time it takes to solve a fixed goal', and the useful range 'typically spans several orders of magnitude'. Kouvaris et al. 2017 (https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005358), table item (b): 'Both high and low time-scales can lead to inflexible developmental structures'. Clune et al. 2013 (https://arxiv.org/abs/1207.2743) fig. 4b spans 10 to 1e4 generations between changes, and connection cost wins 'when rates of environmental change are too slow for the MVG effect to be strong'. Parter et al. 2008 used E = 20 and report that a wide range of E gives similar results.

findings.claim: A connection cost alone makes modularity (and hierarchy) evolve even in a fixed environment. It also makes later adaptation 20x faster, and it adds to MVG. Learning theory reads this as regularisation: varied environments are the training set, and sparsity and noise prevent over-fitting.
findings.evidence: Clune, Mouret & Lipson 2013: performance-plus-connection-cost (P&CC) networks adapted L-AND-R -> L-OR-R in a median 3.0 generations against 65 for performance-only (L-OR-R -> L-AND-R: 12 against 222.5). The cost objective counted only with probability p (stochastic Pareto). Mengistu et al. 2016 (https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1004829): the cost also gives hierarchy. Ellefsen et al. 2015 (https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1004128): the cost gives modules that forget less. Kouvaris 2017: environmental noise and connection cost (L1 better than L2 for modular problems) favour generalised developmental structures.

findings.claim: Evolving under modular variation generalises: populations adapt quickly to new combinations of old subgoals, and even to a subgoal never seen before. The capacity decays within tens of generations once the goal is held fixed.
findings.evidence: Parter, Kashtan & Alon 2008 (full text, https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1000206): logic circuits and RNA, goals switched every 20 generations by a random walk over the modular variants. Facilitated variation decreased 'rapidly within a few tens of generations' under a fixed goal with slight size pressure.

findings.claim: Stepping stones: complex functions evolve when simpler functions that are part of them are also rewarded. Mutations that were harmful when they appeared can be stepping stones.
findings.evidence: Lenski et al. 2003 (abstract opened, https://doi.org/10.1038/nature01568): 'Complex functions evolved by building on simpler functions that had evolved earlier, provided that these were also selectively favoured.' The counts (EQU in 23 of 50 populations with graded rewards, none when only EQU paid) are from my memory of the main text, which is paywalled; I did not re-verify them here.

findings.claim: Evolvability itself evolves in changing environments: a few hub mutations become able to switch the whole expression pattern, and populations are pushed to mutational neighbourhoods rich in alternative phenotypes. This needs large populations, and harsh changes (bottlenecks) work better than benign ones.
findings.evidence: Crombach & Hogeweg 2008 (https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1000112): the environment switched with probability 3e-4 per step; hubs switched expression with few indels; small lattices lost evolvability to Muller's ratchet. Draghi & Wagner 2008 abstract: changing environments favour a variability pattern that maximises evolvability, and nonrandom change selects modular variability. Earl & Deem 2004 (https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0404656101): rapid or dramatic change selects for evolvability. Canino-Koning et al. 2019 (https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1006445): 1,000-update cycles (~30 generations) for 200 cycles; harsh changes cause bottlenecks and more phenotype switching, while static environments select 'solely for immediate optimization'.

findings.claim: How often to switch, within a life: learning or reversible plasticity evolves when (a) the best action changes between or within lives, (b) experience reliably signals the current state, (c) the state lasts within the life, and (d) the fixed alternatives earn about the same. Fast change with unreliable cues favours bet-hedging, which here means a generalist reflex. Slow change favours genetic tracking. Rare change favours stochastic switching over paying for sensing all the time.
findings.evidence: Stephens 1991 abstract (https://doi.org/10.1093/beheco/2.1.77): within-generation persistence matters most, and learning is 'most useful when all the alternatives to learning yield about the same payoff'. Dunlap & Stephens 2009 (https://doi.org/10.1098/rspb.2009.0602), Drosophila over 30 generations: unpredictable best action with reliable experience (p 0.5, q 1.0) strongly favours learning; a fixed best action with unreliable experience (p 1.0, q 0.5) strongly disfavours it; p = q = 1 is neutral. Botero et al. 2015 (https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1408589111): R (generations per environmental cycle) and cue predictability P partition the responses into reversible plasticity, irreversible plasticity, bet-hedging and tracking, and plasticity evolved only when individuals could anticipate the change. Kussell & Leibler 2005 abstract: stochastic switching beats sensing when the environment changes rarely.

findings.claim: The lifetime-learning precedents give each context tens of consequence events, put several contexts in one life, randomise the meaning in every life, and feed the reward or consequence to the network as an input.
findings.evidence: Soltoggio et al. 2008 (full text, https://infoscience.epfl.ch/record/121548): 100 (single) or 200 (double T-maze) trials per life; high reward 1.0 against 0.2, moved after about 50 +- 15 trials; reward is a network input; modulated plasticity beat fixed-weight networks by a wide margin. Ellefsen 2015: in every life two of four foods are randomly nutritious, with reward and punishment inputs, 4 random lives per individual in evolution and 80 at test. Wang et al. 2016 (https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.05763) and Duan et al. 2016 (https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.02779): a memory network trained over interrelated tasks, given the previous reward and action as inputs, learns in its activations with frozen weights and exploits the task-family structure.

findings.claim: Searching for learning is deceptive: static heuristics earn reward sooner, so plain fitness search tends to settle on non-adaptive policies. This is the literature's name for the generalist-reflex collapse.
findings.evidence: Risi, Hughes & Stanley 2010 abstract (https://doi.org/10.1177/1059712310379923): 'learning to learn is highly deceptive. Because it is easier at first to improve fitness without evolving the ability to learn, evolution is likely to exploit domain-dependent static (i.e., nonadaptive) heuristics'; novelty search found stepping stones that fitness search missed.

findings.claim: In machine learning, in-context (within-episode) learning appears only past a threshold of task diversity, needs contexts that persist within an episode ('burstiness') and many rare classes, is limited by state (memory) size, and trades off against storing the answer in the weights.
findings.evidence: Raventós et al. 2023 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.15063): a 'task diversity threshold', below which the model acts as a Bayesian estimator with the training tasks as prior. Chan et al. 2022 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.05055): burstiness, many rare classes and dynamic meanings drive in-context learning, with a tradeoff against in-weights learning that a Zipfian mix resolves. Kirsch et al. 2022 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.04458): transitions between memorising, generalising and failing with model size and number of tasks, long plateaus, and capability 'bottlenecked by the accessible state size'.

findings.claim: Curricula and open-ended methods converge on one selection rule: keep tasks at the frontier (not too easy, not too hard), score them by regret against a capable reference, build new ones by small edits of high-regret tasks, and let solutions transfer between tasks. Uniform domain randomisation adds no structure; adversarial worst-case tasks are unsolvable.
findings.evidence: POET (https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.01753): minimal criterion 50 <= E_child <= 300; transfer between environments is essential; many of its environments cannot be solved by direct optimisation or a direct-path curriculum. Enhanced POET (https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.08536): PATA-EC and the ANNECS progress measure. PAIRED (https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.02096): domain randomisation 'cannot generate structure', minimax gives unsolvable worlds, and regret = antagonist minus protagonist return. PLR (https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.03934): TD-error scores plus staleness. ACCEL (https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.01302): small edits to high-regret levels. OMNI (https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.01711): a learning-progress filter alone leaves 'countless learnable yet uninteresting tasks'. AdA (https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.07608): adaptation needs a diverse task distribution, a memory architecture and a curriculum at the agent's frontier; uniform sampling did worse.

findings.claim: Minimal-cognition work offers a ready catalogue of CATCH-like tasks that demand more than reflexes: catch circles and avoid diamonds (discrimination by active scanning), catch objects blind (predict and remember), switch attention between two objects, and a fixed-weight network that learns which sequence pays.
findings.evidence: Beer 1996 and 2003 (abstracts, https://doi.org/10.7551/mitpress/3118.003.0051, https://doi.org/10.1177/1059712303114001). Slocum, Downey & Beer 2000 (abstract, https://doi.org/10.7551/mitpress/3120.003.0046): agents 'predict and remember the future location of objects in order to catch them blind, and switch their attention between multiple distal objects'. Yamauchi & Beer 1994 (abstract): learning a sequence from reinforcement with no explicit learning rule, using a modular GA. Tuci et al. 2002 (abstract): learning without an external reinforcement signal, driven by ecological contingencies. Agmon & Beer 2014 (abstract): action switching driven by internal variables.

findings.claim: Memory and hidden units evolve only when the senses leave an information gap at the moment of action. Fitness then tracks information beyond the sensors, which can be measured directly.
findings.evidence: Albantakis et al. 2014 (full text, https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003966): animats with two sensors and a 1-unit blind spot, 60,000 generations; integration rises with environmental complexity, 'especially on the requirement for sequential memory', and Task 4 needs >= 3 time steps of memory. Marstaller, Hintze & Adami 2013 (https://arxiv.org/abs/1206.5771): representation R = I(E:M|S), information about the environment in internal states beyond the sensors, grows with fitness. Edlund et al. 2011 abstract: integrated information predicts fitness best when the task needs memory.

findings.claim: Measured (this session, existing keys, no repo edits): no existing body, hand-built or evolved, can tell a narrow target from a wide decoy. A wide decoy with the same peak brightness, even when clicking it is free, cuts the tuned reflex's captures from 20.8 to 5.5 per life (F +8.55 -> +0.61). An equal-glow decoy (wide and dim) halves captures (11.1, F +3.62). The router and s5 lose as much or more.
findings.evidence: decoy_headroom.py, 128 lives per condition, seeds fresh_seeds(128, seed0=40,300,000), common random numbers, catch_speck_l4 with sigma 0.6 and b2_sigma 1.2 in b2_mode 0. Paired loss at price 0, wide-bright decoy: reflex@hollow3 -7.94 +- 0.25, router@ring4 -11.88 +- 0.26, s5 -8.82 +- 0.23. Equal-glow decoy (b2_amp 0.25): -4.93, -7.29, -4.74. Router lead over the reflex: base +2.10 +- 0.28; A_0 -1.83 +- 0.13; C_0 -0.25 +- 0.21.

findings.claim: Measured: the decoy's price only re-bills the same lives. Bodies cannot sense value, so within-life adaptation to 'which blob pays' needs a visible consequence. The kernel already provides one: in b2_mode 0, clicking the decoy leaves it in place, while a capture re-places both blobs.
findings.evidence: Captures, misses and decoy clicks are identical across prices 0/25/100/400 under CRN. F falls exactly by decoy clicks/1024 per unit of price (reflex 0.0797 = 81.6/1024; router 0.0268; s5 0.0161). The re-placement rule is in LIFE_ABI.md 9.7.4: a capture defers PLACE(0) and, in mode 0, PLACE(1); a b2 click re-places only in mode 1.

findings.claim: Measured: the price at which the reflex earns nothing (Stephens' 'equal payoff' point) is about 8 per click for the wide-bright decoy and about 88 for the equal-glow decoy (router 108, s5 92). At price 100 the router and s5 beat the reflex (+3.5 and +3.7 F), but only because they click less. That is click gating, which a re-tuned reflex can probably match with one centre-cell change. The pursuit loss, which needs a spatial circuit, is common to all three bodies.
findings.evidence: decoy_analysis.json. Clicks on the wide decoy per life: reflex 81.6, router 27.4, s5 16.5. Paired leads in A_100: router +3.46 +- 0.18, s5 +3.73 +- 0.17. Mixes: 50% base + 50% A_25 gives reflex +3.59 against an upper bound of +8.55 (a perfect decoy-ignorer, measured as the no-decoy world), router +4.38 (bound +10.66), s5 +2.20 (bound +6.81). Caveat: the bodies were tuned in base SPECK and not re-tuned here.

findings.claim: Measured: swapping which halo width pays between lives is a badly unbalanced family. A wide target (sigma 1.2) makes SPECK easy for the reflex (+19.2, 43 captures) but not for the narrow-tuned router (+8.2) or s5 (+6.3). Such a family needs a fixed per-world normalisation, or equal-difficulty variants.
findings.evidence: B0: reflex +19.24 +- 0.30, router +8.21 (paired -11.03 +- 0.32), s5 +6.26. Swap A_100/B_100: reflex +3.96 against bound +13.89, router +1.47 against +9.43, s5 0.00 against +6.53.

findings.claim: Event budget, from project numbers: base SPECK gives about 20.8 captures per 1,024 units, one about every 49 units. The learning precedents use tens of consequence events per context, so learning from captures alone could support only about 2 epochs per life. Denser signals are available: clicks (45-120 per life), decoy encounters, and reafference (each twitch changes the receptor stream within ~1-2 units).
findings.evidence: reflex@hollow3 base: captures 20.8, misses 45.4 per life (decoy_headroom.log). Soltoggio 2008: about 50 trials per context, 2-4 contexts per life. Ellefsen 2015: days x seasons x years with every item seen daily. A motor-sign flip shows itself through reafference without any reward bit; 'which blob pays' needs click outcomes (persistence after a click) or the pending local consequence signal.

findings.claim: Design rules mapped to this project, in brief. R1 shared structure: L1 axes should recombine sub-skills (approach/avoid by halo type, lead direction), not only change difficulty (halo width, noise), which is domain randomisation and in the pilot mostly selected 'be smaller'. R2 temporal MVG: add an arm in which the world's combination flips for the whole population every E generations (try E in {10, 30, 100}; first measure the generations needed to recover after a switch), compared against the simultaneous L1 mixture. R3 within-life epochs: several per life, each holding tens of locally visible consequence events, with the price near the static policy's break-even. R4 against collapse: pick worlds by regret of a hand-built computing body over the re-tuned reflex, apply a POET-style minimal criterion to the current champion, keep stepping-stone lives (base SPECK 25-50%), and ramp complexity by small edits of high-regret worlds. R5 keep message costs and do not raise c_live; a wiring cost is optional and needs approval. R6 memory worlds need information gaps. R7 within-life learning needs randomised meaning in every life, many distinct contexts, and a consequence the cell can see. R8 always measure against a control that removes the capability (genes_blind = Soltoggio's fixed-weight control; lateral_off; hidden_off), plus re-adaptation time, held-out combinations, R = I(E:M|S), and a count of world variants in which the body beats the re-tuned reflex (like ANNECS).
findings.evidence: Synthesised from the sources above. Project facts are from docs/POST_PILOT_CALLS.md: the twin target shrank the router's lead from +2.17 to +0.37; split-half reliability rose from 0.18 to 0.5 mostly through 'be smaller'; at c_live 0.04 the router's lead fell from +2.25 to about +0.93 and reversed at 0.06; the population-triggered c_miss ramp was dropped as a designer schedule. A fixed periodic switch every E generations does not respond to the population, so it is an environment property, unlike the dropped ramp.

candidates.name: WIDTH-DECOY family (Beer's catch-circles-avoid-diamonds on existing b2 keys)
candidates.capability: (5) discrimination, with (1) lateral routing as the mechanism and (2) a short memory of the last click as an add-on
candidates.world_change: Existing keys only. Per-life family: 25-50% base SPECK lives (stepping stones); the rest are A-type lives with b2_amp 1.0, b2_sigma 1.2 (wide, same peak as the target, sigma 0.6), b2_mode 0, b2_value -v with v in about 8-100 (around the reflex break-even), b2_rho 1.0. Optional ramp via b2_p or b2_amp as fixed family members (ACCEL-style small edits), not a population-triggered schedule. Prefer the same-peak decoy over the equal-glow one: the equal-glow decoy can be told apart by a single cell's event-rate threshold (a one-cell solution).
candidates.why_reflex_fails: The reflex pulls toward any glow. A wide decoy lights more sensors and more receptor events than the narrow target, so it captures pursuit and clicking: captures 20.8 -> 5.5 and 81.6 decoy clicks per life even at price 0. At equal peak, no per-cell threshold can tell the two apart.
candidates.minimal_circuit: Centre-surround at 1-2 hops. Each sensor excites the act cell above it (the reflex) and inhibits neighbouring columns' act cells or sensors on channel 1. A narrow halo (luminance 0.25 at 1 hop, 0.004 at 2 hops) drives a column with a quiet surround; a wide halo (0.71 at 1 hop, 0.25 at 2) lights the surround, which vetoes the pull and the click. Add-on: a hotspot latch that suppresses re-clicking a blob that survived a click (b2_mode 0 leaves the decoy in place).
candidates.positive_control: A hand role body on ring3/hollow3 (handbuilt.role_body) whose sensors also emit on channel 1, with lateral channel-1 weights negative at act cells (or sensors), tuned with analysis.tune_knobs on the mixed family. Compare it with the reflex re-tuned on the same family; the re-tune is essential because a reflex with a slower clicker already removes most of the click cost. Gate: centre-surround minus re-tuned reflex >= 3 SE on 1,024 paired lives, with the lead coming from captures (pursuit), not only from fewer decoy clicks.
candidates.measurement: F paired against the re-tuned reflex per world type. Capture and decoy-click counts. Psychophysics as in Beer 2003: sweep b2_sigma from 0.6 to 1.5 and record approach and click probability per blob. lateral_off share of F (prediction: most of the lead disappears). P.chains rec_other_col: inhibitory chains starting in neighbouring columns. P.lesion of channel-1 lateral slots.
candidates.engineering: None for the world (b2_* already exist in kernel.c, reference.py and lifesim.js). A family draw per life in evaluate.py (the planned L1 harness). Building and tuning the hand body: about a day.
candidates.risks: Lives where the reflex loses money push toward 'be smaller / do nothing' unless stepping-stone lives keep it positive (measured: 50% base + 50% A_25 gives reflex +3.6 against a bound of +8.6). The decoy price must stay near break-even (8 per click for the bright decoy). A re-tuned reflex with gated clicking may recover part of the gap. The upper bound (+8 F) is a no-decoy world, not a built body.
candidates.evidence_or_result: Measured 128 lives per condition, seeds fresh_seeds(128, 40,300,000), CRN. Loss to a free wide decoy: reflex -7.94 +- 0.25, router -11.88 +- 0.26, s5 -8.82 +- 0.23; equal-glow decoy -4.93 / -7.29 / -4.74. No existing body discriminates (router lead A_0 -1.83 +- 0.13). Break-even price: reflex 8 (bright), 88 (equal-glow). Prices only re-bill (behaviour identical across prices).

candidates.name: MVG-SWAP: which halo type pays flips every E generations (Kashtan modularly varying goals)
candidates.capability: (4) context switching at the evolutionary timescale; evolvability and modular structure (a width module plus an approach-sign module)
candidates.world_change: A harness world clock: generations g in [kE, (k+1)E) use phase k mod 2. Phase 0 is narrow pays / wide costs (A-type: sigma 0.6, b2_sigma 1.2, b2_value -v); phase 1 is wide pays / narrow costs. Phase 1 needs sigma 1.2 with b2_sigma 0.6; normalise per phase, or reduce lam_s in phase 1 to equalise difficulty, because a wide target is much easier. Lives within a generation keep CRN and are drawn from the current phase only. E in {10, 30, 100}. Controls: a fixed goal (phase 0 only) and the simultaneous mixture (both phases every generation, Kashtan's multiobjective control).
candidates.why_reflex_fails: The reflex approaches both types equally in both phases. Its mean is set by whichever blob is cheaper and it cannot switch, so selection keeps rewarding any heritable width discrimination plus an approach sign that one mutation can flip.
candidates.minimal_circuit: The centre-surround width detector (shared module) plus one GRN weight that sets whether 'narrow' or 'wide' drives approach or avoidance: Kashtan's AND <-> OR combiner between two persistent modules.
candidates.positive_control: The WIDTH-DECOY hand body and its sign-flipped twin, both scored in both phases, show headroom in each phase. For reachability, seed a population with the hand genome and measure how many generations it takes to recover after a switch (Kashtan: 3-5 for modular solutions).
candidates.measurement: Generations to reach a fixed F bar, against the fixed-goal arm and the simultaneous-mixture arm (speedup S = T_fixed / T_MVG). Re-adaptation time after each switch. Functional modularity (lateral_off and channel lesions per role). Generalisation to a held-out combination (Parter 2008), e.g. a moving decoy with a different speed.
candidates.engineering: Harness only: a phase function of the generation in evaluate.py / evolve.py and a config key. No kernel, reference or JS change, because each life's world is ordinary b2_* keys.
candidates.risks: Must be justified as an environment property (fixed period, independent of population state) to avoid the 'designer schedule' objection. Noise (per-life SD ~2 F) can make phases chase noise; needs paired lives. The phase asymmetry needs per-phase normalisation (measured: B0 reflex +19.2 against A0 +8.6). If E is shorter than the re-adaptation time, populations bet-hedge (Botero) and the reflex wins.
candidates.evidence_or_result: No MVG run done. Literature: MVG speedup 10x to 1e3x, growing with goal difficulty; the simultaneous multiobjective control gave 'virtually no speedup'; E = 20 worked, with a window spanning orders of magnitude. Project measurement: the swap mean at v = 100 is reflex +3.96 against a decoy-ignoring bound of +13.89.

candidates.name: EPOCHS with visible consequences (within-life switching, L2)
candidates.capability: (4) within-life adaptation and context switching; (2) persistence (state set by a consequence and held through the epoch)
candidates.world_change: New world feature: at Poisson world times (mean 200-300 units, 3-5 switches per life at T 1024, or T 2048 if events are too few), swap sigma <-> b2_sigma (which width pays) or flip the motor sign (g_n -> -g_n). Prefer the motor flip first: the reflex earns negatively in flipped epochs, and the flip is visible through reafference within ~1-2 units of any twitch. 'Which blob pays' is visible only through click outcomes (in b2_mode 0 the decoy persists after a click), at roughly 45-120 clicks per life.
candidates.why_reflex_fails: A fixed policy is right in one context and wrong in the other. With the price near break-even, its mean is about 0 (Stephens' equal-payoff condition), so only a body that tracks the context earns.
candidates.minimal_circuit: A context latch: a cell state (membrane hold or gene expression) set by a local mismatch. For the motor flip: a twitch toward the active side followed by the halo moving outward. For which-pays: a click followed by a persistent blob. The latch gates the sign of sensor-to-act transmission (motor flip) or which width is approached. It needs no global signal.
candidates.positive_control: A hand GRN body (handbuilt.router_genome-style raw genome) with one context gene that a local mismatch sets and that inverts act-cell input weights. It must beat both the re-tuned reflex and a fixed best guess on a 50/50 epoch mixture by >= 3 SE. The genes_blind fork after development must remove the gain (Soltoggio's fixed-weight control).
candidates.measurement: Post-switch recovery curve, F per epoch-quarter. Recovery latency against epoch length. A genes_blind or membrane-reset fork at the switch. R = I(context : cell state | receptor events) from probe traces. Paired lives.
candidates.engineering: kernel.c, reference.py and lifesim.js (scalar world redraws at Poisson world times; the review estimated 30-50 kernel lines), new world keys (from the reserved range, ABI bump), a bitwise test of kernel = reference = JS, and probe support for epoch boundaries.
candidates.risks: Too few consequence events per epoch (captures about every 49 units); a switch faster than detection selects bet-hedging, which here is the generalist reflex (Botero). Deception: static heuristics win early (Risi 2010), so keep non-switching stepping-stone lives. The 'which blob pays' version may need the pending local consequence signal if persistence-after-click proves too weak.
candidates.evidence_or_result: No epoch world run (needs new keys). Measured analogue: the decoy's price is invisible to bodies (identical behaviour at prices 0-400 under CRN), and the only existing consequence cue is the b2_mode-0 persistence after a click. Literature precedent: about 50 consequence events per context and 2-4 contexts per life (Soltoggio 2008); experience reliability q = 1 with best-action fixity p = 0.5 favours learning (Dunlap & Stephens 2009).

candidates.name: BLINK / catch-blind (information gap gives the hidden planes a job)
candidates.capability: (2) memory and persistence; (3) prediction and interception
candidates.world_change: New feature: the target's glow switches off for Poisson gaps (e.g. 3-10 units, a few times per placement) while it keeps moving. Raise v_t and tau_turn (faster, straighter targets) so the position at reappearance is predictable from the pre-gap motion. Existing-key partial version: higher v_t with long tau_turn (prediction only, no gap).
candidates.why_reflex_fails: With no receptor events during a gap, the reflex stops pulling. Its only memory is s4-style post-spike reset (about 1.8 units). A target moving straight at v_t drifts out of the footprint.
candidates.minimal_circuit: A per-column reverberating hold (sensor -> act -> hidden cell -> back down to act) that keeps the last pull direction for several units, decaying by leak. Or a delay-line comparator between neighbouring sensors (direction from timing) that biases the pull ahead of the target.
candidates.positive_control: Extend handbuilt.hold_body (the existing 2-hop centre hold) to every rim column with a hidden-plane loop. Gate as in POST_PILOT_CALLS L4: it must beat the re-tuned reflex by >= 3 SE, and hidden_off during gaps must remove the lead.
candidates.measurement: hidden_off fork during gaps. R = I(E:M|S) (Marstaller 2013) with E the target's direction during the gap, M the hidden and act states, S the receptor events. Capture rate as a function of gap length. Albantakis-style counts of cells that carry information about the target.
candidates.engineering: kernel.c, reference.py and lifesim.js (a gap schedule on blob luminance: one Poisson stream and a halo multiplier), world keys and an ABI bump, tests.
candidates.risks: The pilot's occlusion test gained only +0.05 and a single slow cell matched it, so gaps must be long relative to single-cell time constants (tau_m up to 16) and the target must move. Memory headroom may be small at SPECK capture rates. Gaps also cost all bodies equally, so the fitness scale shrinks.
candidates.evidence_or_result: No run. Literature: memory and integration evolve only when the task needs sequential memory (Albantakis 2014: blind spot between sensors, Task 4 needs >= 3 steps); catching blind is an established minimal-cognition task (Slocum, Downey & Beer 2000).

candidates.name: Regret-curated family (PAIRED / POET minimal criterion / ACCEL edits over existing keys)
candidates.capability: Any of (1)-(6); this is a method for choosing the variation so it rewards computation over the generalist reflex
candidates.world_change: Existing keys only. Build the L1 family from world variants (b2_* decoys, sigma, v_t, tau_turn, lam_bg, kill_t/kill_frac, c_miss) kept only where a hand-built computing body beats the re-tuned reflex (positive regret, the PAIRED 'antagonist') and where the current evolved champion scores inside a fixed band (POET minimal criterion: not too easy, not too hard). New variants are small edits of high-regret ones (ACCEL). Recompute only at fixed checkpoints (e.g. every 100 generations), using a fixed rule. Keep base SPECK at 25-50% of lives as the stepping stone.
candidates.why_reflex_fails: By construction, worlds where the reflex already earns most of the reward (the twin target, near placement, the router's -1.28 sparse-receptor case) are excluded or down-weighted, so no family-wide mean rewards the reflex for free.
candidates.minimal_circuit: Depends on the variant: centre-surround (decoys), a hold loop (gaps), contact-count regrowth (wounds).
candidates.positive_control: The hand bodies are the antagonists: router@ring4 for routing, the centre-surround body for decoys, a hold body for memory. Each is re-tuned per variant alongside the reflex.
candidates.measurement: Per-variant regret table (antagonist minus re-tuned reflex, and evolved minus re-tuned reflex). An ANNECS-like count of variants where the evolved body beats the re-tuned reflex by >= 3 SE. lateral_off share across the family as the guard from POST_PILOT_CALLS L1.
candidates.engineering: Harness and scripts (a niche-map script plus a family table read by evaluate.py); no kernel change for existing keys.
candidates.risks: A family chosen by checkpoint is a schedule; keep it rule-based and population-blind except through the fixed band, or freeze it after the niche map. Re-tuning the reflex per variant is costly (300 evaluations, about 10-20 min each). Variety that mostly selects 'be smaller' must be watched (end-size correlation).
candidates.evidence_or_result: Measured in this session: the decoy variants have large regret against all existing bodies (no-decoy bound about +8 F over the reflex in A-type lives); the wide-target variant B0 favours the reflex (+19.2 against the router's +8.2), so B0 is a 'too easy for the reflex' variant to exclude or normalise.

candidates.name: WOUND lives as a modular variant (L3 inside the family)
candidates.capability: (6) regeneration and size regulation; gives genome-driven death a job
candidates.world_change: Existing panel keys kill_t (rel) and kill_frac drawn per life (e.g. kill_t in [T/4, T/2], kill_frac in 0.25-0.5) in 20-30% of family lives. kill_rate (reserved, Poisson per cell) later.
candidates.why_reflex_fails: The hand reflex never regrows: its program cells do not divide, so a wound costs it permanently. Evolved stoppers regrow only 0-35% of a 25% wound (pilot baseline).
candidates.minimal_circuit: Contact-count-gated division: the n_view brake that stops growth releases when neighbours die, so rim cells re-divide into the gap. s2 already raises gain when a neighbour dies (in-life adaptation over 10-100 units).
candidates.positive_control: handbuilt.column_grower or column_genome with a growth window: it should regrow to the same disk after kill_frac 0.25-0.5, F measured against the same body without regrowth.
candidates.measurement: Fraction of cells regrown by T; F lost to the wound, with and without the regrowth path (n_view knockout); time to recover pre-wound capture rate.
candidates.engineering: None for kill_t/kill_frac (they exist in kernel.c, reference.py and lifesim.js as panel keys). Family draw in the harness. kill_rate needs an ABI change.
candidates.risks: Wounds may mostly select smaller bodies (less to lose) rather than regrowth. Mixed with decoys it can confound. Literature support here is indirect: modular variation and harsh changes (Canino-Koning 2019: bottlenecks increase evolvability).
candidates.evidence_or_result: No run in this session. Project baseline from docs/POST_PILOT_CALLS.md L3: stoppers regrow 0-35% of a 25% wound; p_die knockouts are 0.00 everywhere.

findings.claim: Most of the task variety (wounds, two blob types told apart by size, brightness, value or presence, fast or straight-moving targets, and halo, noise, placement and price axes) is already pure config in kernel.c and reference.py. A world: {...} override or a held-out override list sets it today.
findings.evidence: spec.World has kill_t/kill_frac (panel, 7.9), b2_amp/b2_sigma/b2_value/b2_rho/b2_p/b2_mode (9.7.3-9.7.5), v_t and tau_turn (0 = straight). LifeEvaluator.world() merges cfg.world into every life. exp1 (kernel, 128 paired lives, catch_speck_l4, seeds 40,400,000+s) ran all of them on reflex@hollow3, router@ring4, s4, s5 and s7, with sensible ledgers (kills, b2_clicks, captures).

findings.claim: The browser engine lifesim.js supports none of the existing variation keys. Its constructor throws on kill_t >= 0, b2_amp > 0, noise_rate, stuck_t, drop_p and window_h. Each one needs a port and new truth lives before it can be shown in the playground.
findings.evidence: results/atlas/play/lifesim.js lines 552-553 throw the 'panel perturbations ... and the second blob are not supported' error. There is no KILL handler (grep). In auto mode it reads blobs[0] only (P.rate). N_STREAMS = 26 (streams 0..26 are precomputed).

findings.claim: A two-state telegraph epoch process plus square-wave flicker, added on the world side, costs +86/-11 kernel lines. It is bitwise neutral when off and bitwise equal to a Python-reference mirror when on. Heap = window scheduler, and tie, order and salt invariance hold. It covers (b) epochs, (c) blink, (d) motor sign flip, (e) payoff switch, (g) a flicker cue and (h) fast phases.
findings.evidence: scratch kernel_x.c (make_kernel_x.py, kernel_x.diff) adds 12 world keys (66-77), stream S_EPOCH = 26 and fold word 14. exp2: 35/35 body x world cells (7 bodies x 5 worlds x 32 lives = 1,120 lives) match the repo kernel bitwise in ledger, 5 hashes, raster and fate log. exp3: kernel_x = xref.py (a subclass of reference._Life/_Accountant) bitwise in 90/90 lives with features on (flip, blink, swap+cue, fast phase, flicker; reflex, router, s4, s5). Reference speed is 4-40 s per life. exp5: 16/16 heap-vs-window and tie/order/salt comparisons are bitwise with features on.

findings.claim: Only accountant-side world keys may switch within a life. lambda_max (the cell-side receptor candidate rate) must be fixed per life as the maximum over all states. Prices must not switch, or the ledger identity breaks. Payoff swaps stay consistent if 'captures' counts rewarded clicks and 'b2_clicks' counts the other blob.
findings.evidence: A grep of kernel.c shows every CATCH key except lambda_max read only in accountant functions (lines 1200-1550 and close). tau_z and d0 are also read in cell handlers (lines 665, 676, 762). Cell handlers would see stale values under the window scheduler. close_life recomputes cost from price x column and sets ST_MISMATCH on disagreement. The prototype books swapped payoffs into the existing columns: no mismatch bits, and the reference agrees bitwise.

findings.claim: The new manipulations open large F gaps for the reference bodies. That is headroom only if a hand-built adaptive, memory or discriminating body can recover part of it.
findings.evidence:
exp4 (kernel_x, 128 paired lives, seeds 40,403,000+s), dF against base:
- Motor flip with 100/100 dwell: reflex -5.48±0.26, router -7.65, s4 -3.93, s5 -5.33, s7 -4.98. Always flipped: reflex 0 captures.
- Blink 40/10 (20% dark): reflex -2.09, s5 -2.06. Blink 20/20: reflex -5.02, router -7.29, s5 -4.88.
- Fast phase (x3 speed, 60/30 dwell): -1.7 to -2.8.
- Same-size decoy (no cue): reflex -10.57. If the decoy flickers (1-unit half period): -6.28. If the target flickers: -14.56.
- Payoff swap with a background cue and a big decoy: reflex -12.52, s7 -16.04.

findings.claim: A background-rate context cue is not free. Raising lam_bg x6 doubles misses because the click sensor fires on background events. Cue design has to be measured.
findings.evidence: exp4: flip100 against flip100_cue misses go 43.5 -> 89.1 (reflex), 26.7 -> 105.6 (s4) and 16.3 -> 66.6 (s5), so the cue costs a further -0.5 to -0.75 F.

findings.claim: Blob size is a strong existing discrimination axis. With equal peak rate, a big decoy (sigma 1.5) draws most clicks from every body. No single cell can tell a big blob from a small one, but surround suppression can, so this is a candidate niche where lateral computation pays.
findings.evidence: exp1 decoy_big (b2_sigma 1.5, b2_value -500, own timer): reflex -32.87±0.42 F (52 decoy clicks/life), router -24.29, s4 -24.62, s5 -15.61, s7 -26.81. If the big blob pays +500 instead, the reflex gains +18.06. The same-size decoy (no local cue) costs the reflex -9.59: the control.

findings.claim: Fast targets alone do not create an interception niche. By v_t 0.4 chasing no longer beats sitting still: the 2-cell clicker matches the reflex and beats s5.
findings.evidence:
exp8 (128 lives, seeds 40,405,000+s), F at v_t 0.1 / 0.2 / 0.3 / 0.4 / 0.4 straight / 0.8 straight:
- reflex: +8.51 / +6.23 / +3.32 / +0.67 / -0.28 / -1.31
- clicker: +0.47 / +0.78 / +0.72 / +0.61 / +0.43 / +0.07
- s5: +6.50 / +4.36 / +1.44 / -1.03 / -1.91 / -2.65
A lead/interception world needs a hand interceptor that beats the clicker as well as the reflex.

findings.claim: Wounds are pure config, but only GRN bodies regrow. Hand role bodies (program mode, no division) cannot, so a regeneration positive control must be a GRN body.
findings.evidence:
exp1, kill_frac 0.25 / 0.5 at t 512, dF:
- reflex: -3.55 / -4.15
- router: -5.26 / -5.85
- s4: -2.16 / -3.08
- s5: -2.72 / -3.98
- s7: -2.74 / -3.76
Cells regrown by T: s4 42% / 35%, s5 37% / 42%, s7 8% / 12%, hand bodies 0%. A wound is an exact fork by replay: the same life with kill_t set equals its twin before kill_t, so a t_open = kill_t comparison is paired.

findings.claim: A task family per life fits LifeEvaluator as about 110 lines without touching the kernel, and CRN holds. The member id rides in World.name, so recheck_draw's slicing stays aligned.

Random tie-breaking is about 26 lines, neutral when there are no exact ties, and decisive where ties exist. It restores turnover but did not by itself lift frozen v1 populations out of the 1-cell state in 300 generations.
findings.evidence:
scratch evolve_x.py (+26/-5; separate tie generator, permute before each of the three stable sorts):
- Frozen v1 populations lmax4 s7 and s4, 300 gens, run seeds 40,405,000+k: parents-win keeps 0 kids in 300/300 gens (n_tied median 227-230 of 256). Random ties keep 27.5-27.7 kids/gen with 0 frozen gens and drift to 1 breed, but the best stays 1 cell.

findings.claim: Varied worlds cost more CPU per life, mainly through lambda_max (the thinning bound).
findings.evidence: exp4 CPU/life rises 1.5-2.8x in b2 worlds, because lambda_max doubles to 4.05 at b2_amp 1. Background x6 costs about +25%. Base is 0.04 s (reflex) to 0.17 s (s7) on 4 threads of the idle laptop. The exact early receptor rejection (N3) becomes more valuable.

findings.claim: Literature could not be checked in this session.
findings.evidence: WebSearch budget exhausted (200/200), the PNAS fetch returned 403, and the PubMed and arXiv fetches did not return the paper. No literature claim is made.

candidates.capability: Restores neutral drift wherever fitness ties exactly (1-2 cell plateaus, seeded starts, and any rank-based or quantised readout). It is a prerequisite for every variety run.
candidates.world_change: None. Harness only: in src/evolve.py, a tie generator seeded from the run seed and permute-then-stable-sort at lines 361, 368 and 523, plus kids_kept and n_tied in curves rows. The legacy evolve() sort at line 189 can get the same treatment.
candidates.why_reflex_fails: n/a (harness)
candidates.minimal_circuit: n/a
candidates.positive_control: Forced-tie unit test: identical genomes must let children win about half the ties. Resume the frozen v1 populations (s1, s2, s4, s7) with matched RNG.
candidates.measurement: kids_kept and n_tied per generation; generations to more than 4 cells; bitwise-identical curves on a run without exact ties.
candidates.engineering: About 26 lines (prototype +26/-5 in scratch evolve_x.py, minus a test-only init_population hook) plus a unit test: 0.5 person-day. No ABI change.

candidates.name: N2 checkpoint/resume with determinism pinning (harness, do first)
candidates.capability: Long runs (1,000+ gens) and spot-rented portfolios, which variety worlds need because they slow selection.
candidates.why_reflex_fails: n/a
candidates.minimal_circuit: n/a
candidates.positive_control: 6 smoke gens straight against 3 + resume + 3 must be byte-identical (curves with t_gen/t_eval stripped, best_genome.json, population.json, lineage.jsonl), first on one machine, then across two.
candidates.measurement: Byte equality; refusal on an environment fingerprint mismatch.
candidates.engineering: About 120-180 lines (evolve.py about 70, run.py about 40, environment pinning about 30, test about 40): 1-1.5 person-days. No ABI change. The only stateful RNG in the loop is the torch generator; life draws are hash-keyed by (run seed, purpose, index, life).
